paragraphs.heading: A treaty to protect the ozone layer
paragraphs.text: The Montreal Protocol is a worldwide agreement meant to protect the ozone layer. It works by phasing out the making of many chemicals that thin that layer. Countries agreed on it on 16 September 1987, and it took effect on 1 January 1989. It now has 198 parties, 197 states plus the European Union, which made it the first treaty in UN history to win universal ratification.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is called a success
paragraphs.text: Because so many countries signed it and carried it out, it is often held up as a model of nations working together. Kofi Annan, a former UN secretary-general, called it perhaps the most successful international agreement so far. The results show up in the sky: thanks to the treaty, the ozone hole over Antarctica is slowly healing. Projections suggest the ozone layer will be back at its 1980 state in 2040 across much of the world, and in 2066 over Antarctica.

paragraphs.heading: How the rules work
paragraphs.text: The treaty sets controls, deadlines, regular reviews, reporting duties, steps for handling countries that fall short, and help for developing countries. The chemicals it covers are called ozone-depleting substances, or ODSs. They are sorted into groups, each with its own phase-out timetable, and annexes to the treaty list which compounds sit in which group. Article 5 gives developing countries their own obligations, with extra time to meet the controls, and Article 10 sets up a fund to help them comply.

paragraphs.heading: Halons as an example
paragraphs.text: Take the halons: halon-1211, -2404 and -1301. Countries outside Article 5 froze their production and use at 1986 levels on 1 January 1992 and ended them completely by 1994. Article 5 countries froze them on 1 January 2002 at their 1995–97 average, halved them by 2005, and stopped by 2010. A few essential uses with no good substitute at first were exempted; inhalers for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease used to be one. Halon fire suppression in submarines and aircraft also got an exception, though general industry did not.

paragraphs.heading: Decisions guided by experts
paragraphs.text: The parties must base future decisions on current scientific, environmental, technical and economic information, weighed by panels of experts from around the world. A Scientific Assessment Panel reported on ozone depletion in 1989, 1991, 1994, 1998 and 2002. In 1990 the parties also set up a Technology and Economic Assessment Panel (TEAP) to advise them. TEAP reports on alternative technologies that have let harmful ODS use be almost wiped out, and its yearly reports inform what the parties decide.

paragraphs.heading: From CFCs to HCFCs to HFCs
paragraphs.text: HCFCs, or hydrochlorofluorocarbons, are human-made compounds of hydrogen, chlorine, fluorine and carbon that do not occur in nature. Their production took off after countries agreed in the 1980s to stop using CFCs, which were found to be destroying the ozone layer. Most HCFCs break down low in the atmosphere and carry ozone depletion potentials of 0.01–0.5, against 0.6–1.0 for CFCs, yet they are still very potent greenhouse gases. Developed countries set 2020 to end them and developing countries 2030. Since 1 January 2019, the Kigali Amendment has targeted HFCs, which replaced both CFCs and HCFCs, with a promise to cut their use by more than 80% over 30 years.
